results.title: Modelling the Urban Heat Island and Urban Thermal Stress - ENVI-met
results.content: # Modelling the Urban Heat Island and Urban Thermal Stress. #Climate change, #Thermal Comfort, #Urban Heat Island. When discussing the impact of global climate change on our daily life and health, the Urban Heat Island (UHI) effect is often mentioned as an additional source of heat stress for urbanize areas. In fact, the term “Urban Heat Island” can be traced back at least to 1833 when Luke Howard published his book “The climate of London”. In this book, and in thousands of studies by other authors later, this phenomena refers to the fact, that during the night, the urbanized areas are warmer compared to the rural areas. There are many reasons for this and many of them changed over the centuries, but the core reasons for the UHI can be found in missing water evaporation, increased heat storage in buildings and the ground, reduced ventilation and the obstruction of the sky which hinders the heat to escape into the open atmosphere. However, in its original meaning, the Urban Heat Island is a large scale phenomena (Urbanized Areas versus Rural Areas) and it is a night-time effect. Actually, during the day, urban areas in general can be cooler compared to the rural landscape due to the shading effects of buildings. In the last years, especially in the context of climate change adaption of urban areas, the term “Urban Heat Island” is used in a more general and often smaller context to describe the effect of hot spots in urban areas at any time of the day. In a more general way of speaking, we can talk about “Urban Thermal Stress” which includes both the nocturnal effects of the urban environment but also the day-time heat stress elements such as infrared (heat) radiation, reflection and glazing of sun and missing evaporation. With respect to urban planning and architecture, it is important to understand that there is no such thing as “A” urban microclimate. It is therefore inevitable to use numerical simulations to understand which impact urban planning or design decision will have on the open space microclimate. The ENVI-met system allows to analyse the impacts of the local environmental design, such as urban green spaces, selection of ground and building materials or the usage of vegetation on walls or roofs on the urban heat stress for any thinkable configuration.

This study aims to examine the thermal performance of vertical greenery systems (VGS) in composite climates with seasonal fluctuations, focusing on their impact on indoor thermal comfort in naturally ventilated buildings during the monsoon season. Using adequate internal thermal mass (ITM) in buildings is generally regarded as an efficient solution for 'climate responsive architectural design' and 'passive solar design' (Givoni 1992;Shaviv, Yezioro, and Capeluto 2001) , since it can mitigate the fluctuations of indoor thermal dynamics (e.g., indoor air temperature) (Gagliano et al. The thermal storage effect using night ventilation (NV) reduces the peak temperature [3,4], thereby reducing the cooling load [5,6], decreasing electricity consumption [7,8], and improving thermal comfort [9] in buildings with a high thermal mass. This article reviews studies on heat exchange in rooms utilizing radiant cooling systems, including research on conduction in radiant system structures, system cooling loads, cooling capacity, heat transfer coefficients of cooling surfaces, buildings’ thermal performance, and radiant system control strategy, with the goal of maximizing the benefits of energy conservation. The various ways to improve the outdoor thermal environment can be summarized as follows: optimizing community layout and planning to enhance natural ventilation [19][20][21], changing building skin material and color to reduce absorption and storage of solar radiation [22][23][24], implanting various greenery combinations to adjust hot and humid microclimates through transpiration and shading [25][26][27], and integrating shading or green systems onto the original façade to regulate both the interior thermal parameters and exterior microclimate [28][29][30][31][32]. Moreover, thermal inertia properties of materials can be coupled with passive buildings design techniques, e.g. the use of natural ventilation, for lowering indoor daytime temperatures [3,4]. The review also examines PCMs with different natural ventilation strategies, highlighting their potential to enhance indoor thermal comfort and energy efficiency. This study constructs a coupled simulation model of heat balance analysis and computational fluid dynamics (CFD) for naturally ventilated buildings with installed phase change materials (PCMs), and demonstrates a modeling method for the thermal storage effect of PCM in the simulation.

Title: Effect of thermal mass, night ventilation and window shading on summer thermal comfort of buildings in a temperate climate - ScienceDirect
## Building and Environment. Volume 204, 15 October 2021, 108126. # Effect of thermal mass, night ventilation and window shading on summer thermal comfort of buildings in a temperate climate. Author links open overlay panel, , ,. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.buildenv.2021.108126Get rights and content. Under a Creative Commons license. ## Highlights. The study was conducted during 2 heat waves with average maximum temperature 30.1°C and 31.8°C. By combining all the passive methods analyzed, hours with maximum temperatures above 28oC were eliminated. Coupling of high thermal mass with night ventilation eliminated hours with temperature above 31oC. Increasing the thermal mass from light to heavy almost eliminated hours exceeding the absolute Tmax value. Using night ventilation significantly increased the diurnal variations of indoor temperature. ## Abstract. Night ventilation and external blinds are the most commonly used passive methods to protect buildings from overheating during high summer temperatures. Another recommended measure is high thermal inertia of buildings. The aim of the study was to compare the effectiveness of night ventilation, external blinds and thermal mass during a heat wave on the thermal performance of a building during a heat wave in a temperate climate. Increasing the thermal mass of the room from light to very heavy without night ventilation resulted in a reduction of the average peak temperature by 3.7 K in a day and 1.2 K by night. The activation of night ventilation in a light room resulted in a reduction of the average value of the peak temperature by 1.5 K during the day and 5.9 K at night. Increase of thermal mass from light to heavy and night ventilation from 0.6 to 10 ACH led to decrease of average peak temperature by 4.7 K in a day and 4.6 K by night. The simultaneous increase of thermal mass, activation of night ventilation and closing of external blinds resulted in lowering the average peak temperature by 7.4 K in a day and 6.3 K by night. The analysis of the test results indicates that the high thermal mass and the closing of the external blinds reduces the diurnal variations of the indoor temperature, while the activation of nighventilation increases it significantly, especially for lightweight construction.

results.title: Windows and shading solutions for thermal comfort with VELUX
results.content:
Title: Windows and shading solutions for thermal comfort with VELUX
Natural ventilative cooling by opening windows is a very direct and fast method of influencing the thermal environment. * Night ventilation (also referred to as night cooling) will cool down a building's thermal mass at night by using cool outdoor air. Through a combination of measurements and detailed simulations, the effects of ventilative cooling on indoor temperature were determined by the Institute Armines (Favre, 2013). It was even possible to keep the indoor temperature below the outdoor during daytime (especially when the control system in MAL was used), only opening windows when the net effect on thermal comfort was positive. The ventilation flows achieved per window are in the range of 50-100 l/s when 8 roof windows are used for night cooling, and the ventilation rate of the house is in the range of 4-6 ACH. The results in the table show that without night cooling, overheating will occur for 12% of the occupied hours of a year; with night cooling the problem is reduced to 9%, which could be further reduced with solar shading. Using natural ventilation for night cooling thus improves the thermal environment in the house. The use of windows for ventilative cooling and particularly night cooling has been investigated in the VELUX ModelHome 2020 projects. The window openings were controlled automatically to maintain an indoor temperature within category 1 or 2. It is also seen that during the summer, windows were also open during the night, which means that night cooling was part of achieving the good thermal environment (Foldbjerg et al., 2014). An automatic control system for thermal comfort includes those dynamic elements that have an influence on the thermal environment: electric window openers, external shading and/or internal blinds. Its findings are that dynamic shading control can reduce the experienced temperature by up to 7°C in summer and, in most cases, eliminate overheating (or reduce the cooling demand by up to 90%). Automatic control of windows and shading can reduce overheating and the need for mechanical cooling. The solar shading was controlled automatically, based on external solar radiation and indoor temperature. results.title: CFD for Urban Planning: How CFD is Used to Model Wind Flow, Heat Distribution, and Pollutant Dispersion in Urban Environments
results.content:
Title: CFD for Urban Planning: How CFD is Used to Model Wind Flow, Heat Distribution, and Pollutant Dispersion in Urban Environments
CFD for Urban Planning: How CFD is Used to Model Wind Flow, Heat Distribution, and Pollutant Dispersion in Urban Environments. # CFD for Urban Planning: How CFD is Used to Model Wind Flow, Heat Distribution, and Pollutant Dispersion in Urban Environments. CFD allows urban planners and environmental engineers to simulate these complexities, offering insights that can guide the development of more sustainable and livable cities. In summary, the utilization of CFD for wind flow modeling in urban environments empowers urban planners to develop cities that prioritize human well-being and environmental sustainability. Through careful consideration of building geometries, terrain variations, and urban densities, CFD aids in designing cities that harness natural wind flow to mitigate adverse effects and enhance urban livability. CFD models allow urban planners to simulate how different materials contribute to heat retention and gradually release heat into the environment. Through meticulous modeling of building materials, surface albedo, and vegetation, CFD enables the development of effective urban designs that can mitigate UHI effects and promote more comfortable and sustainable urban living conditions. Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) is witnessing increased application in urban planning, particularly in understanding pollutant dispersion and its subsequent impact on air quality. By leveraging CFD, urban planners can simulate complex interactions between pollutant particles and environmental parameters such as wind speed, direction, and temperature variations. CFD modeling helps architects and urban planners identify such phenomena and adapt designs to enhance ventilation and reduce pollutant accumulation. Combining Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) with Geographic Information Systems (GIS) has significantly enhanced the capabilities of urban planning. When integrated with CFD tools, these systems offer a robust framework for simulating urban phenomena such as wind flow, heat distribution, and pollutant dispersion. The spatial data from GIS allowed for an accurate representation of the urban environment, while CFD simulations provided insights into wind patterns and identified areas with poor air circulation. Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) plays a crucial role in urban planning, providing insights into wind flow, heat distribution, and pollutant dispersion. These technologies not only enhance the accuracy and efficiency of CFD simulations but also provide urban planners with the tools they need to create more sustainable and resilient urban environments.
